reason: Attacked hardest of the four, because I found a live textual variant, and it still holds. THE VARIANT: one full reproduction of Scene Seven (a classroom annotation copy) reads 'for time is the longest distance between places', without 'two'. I pulled that page's raw HTML and confirmed the omission is really in it. But that copy is not a witness to the named edition: it is an unidentified retyping that also reads 'shoebox' and 'good-bye' where the American reading text has 'shoe-box', and a dropped 'two' is the commonest kind of transcription slip. Against it, LitCharts, SparkNotes, eNotes, libquotes and The Millions all read 'between two places', and libquotes files it under the 1945 text. The preponderance is decisive and the shipped wording is right; the editor should simply know the variant exists. Publisher correction: confirmed and correct. Bookseller and auction records (Raptis, Burnside, Heritage, Biblio) all give The Glass Menagerie, New York: Random House, 1945 as the first edition, and New Directions 1949 as the reprint carrying the Lustig jacket and the added essay, so there is no New Directions 1945 and the verifier was right to move it. Locator: scene seven, Tom's closing speech, confirmed; the play is in seven scenes in the reading text, and the speech runs on to 'Blow out your candles, Laura'. Speaker named. Attribution: not on the misattribution list. shipped.js: not shipped, no near match, Tennessee Williams at 0 for the year, not banned. Scope: stage play, 1945, publishable, elegiac but not bleak and nothing needing a warning. Mechanics: source line is 89 characters, leads with the name, no em dash and no straight double quote in the source, the quotation's own em dash is permitted since the rule binds only source and note, quotation ends in a full stop, tag Drama is the form. Theme: the August line on time. Limit: I could not open the Random House 1945 sheet itself; a photocopied script PDF I downloaded had no text layer and no PDF renderer is installed here, and the Google Books and archive.org full-text routes were quota-exhausted or dead.
